## Limiting Eigenvalue Distributions of Banded Toeplitz Matrices via Vector Equilibrium Problems

This paper investigates the asymptotic spectral behavior of banded Toeplitz matrices, focusing specifically on the limiting distribution of eigenvalues as the matrix dimension $n$ tends to infinity. Banded Toeplitz matrices—finite-dimensional truncations of Toeplitz operators possessing only a finite number of nonzero diagonals—arise naturally in numerous areas of applied mathematics, including numerical analysis, signal processing, and the study of difference equations, making the understanding of their spectral properties a problem of both theoretical and practical importance.

The foundational work on this topic dates back to the classical results of Schmidt and Spitzer, later complemented by Hirschman, who established that as $n \to \infty$, the eigenvalues of these banded Toeplitz matrices do not spread throughout the complex plane but instead accumulate along a specific, well-defined curve. More precisely, these authors demonstrated that the normalized eigenvalue counting measure—the empirical distribution that assigns equal mass $1/n$ to each eigenvalue—converges weakly to a limiting probability measure supported on this curve. This curve, often referred to in the literature as the Schmidt-Spitzer curve, is determined by the symbol of the Toeplitz matrix and encodes essential information about the spectral asymptotics of the underlying operator family.

While the existence and geometric characterization of this limiting curve have been well understood since these classical contributions, a full characterization of the limiting measure itself—that is, a description not merely of where the eigenvalues accumulate but of how they are distributed along the curve—has remained a more delicate question. The present paper addresses this gap by providing a new characterization of the limiting eigenvalue distribution through the lens of potential theory. Specifically, the authors show that this measure can be described as the unique solution to a suitably formulated equilibrium problem, thereby connecting the spectral theory of banded Toeplitz matrices to the broader framework of logarithmic potential theory and equilibrium measures.

The central result of the paper identifies the limiting eigenvalue measure as one component of a vector of measures that jointly minimize an energy functional defined over the class of admissible vectors of measures. This energy functional incorporates both individual logarithmic energies of the component measures and interaction terms between them, reflecting the coupled nature of the equilibrium problem. The authors prove that this vector energy functional admits a unique minimizer within the appropriate admissible class, and that the first component of this minimizing vector coincides precisely with the limiting spectral measure of the banded Toeplitz matrices originally studied by Schmidt-Spitzer and Hirschman.

Beyond this primary identification, the paper also elucidates the probabilistic and spectral meaning of the remaining components of the minimizing vector of measures. These additional components are shown to correspond to the limiting distributions of normalized counting measures associated with certain generalized eigenvalues—auxiliary spectral quantities that arise naturally in the vector equilibrium framework but do not directly correspond to eigenvalues of the original Toeplitz matrices themselves. This result reveals that the full vector equilibrium problem captures not only the classical eigenvalue distribution but also a richer family of related spectral measures, situating the classical Schmidt-Spitzer-Hirschman theory within a more general and structurally illuminating potential-theoretic context. In this way, the paper both recovers known results and extends them, offering new tools for the analysis of banded Toeplitz matrices and their generalizations.

# Eigenvalue Distributions of Banded Toeplitz Matrices and Vector Equilibrium Problems

## 1. Introduction

The spectral theory of Toeplitz matrices occupies a central place in the study of structured linear operators, with deep connections to approximation theory, orthogonal polynomials, random matrix theory, and mathematical physics. Among the fundamental questions in this area is the behavior of the eigenvalues of finite Toeplitz matrices as the matrix size grows without bound. While the case of banded Toeplitz matrices—those whose symbol is a Laurent polynomial—might appear to be a simple special case, it in fact conceals a rich and subtle structure that has attracted sustained attention since the mid-twentieth century.

This paper is devoted to a precise description of the limiting eigenvalue distribution of $n \times n$ banded Toeplitz matrices $T_n(a)$ as $n \to \infty$, where the symbol
$$
a(z) = \sum_{j=-p}^{q} a_j z^j, \qquad a_{-p} \neq 0, \ a_q \neq 0,
$$
is a fixed Laurent polynomial independent of $n$. Our goal is to characterize the limiting empirical measure of eigenvalues via a variational principle: specifically, through a *vector equilibrium problem* in which the limiting spectral measure appears as one coordinate of the unique minimizer of a suitably defined energy functional acting on tuples of measures. This perspective not only recovers and unifies classical results but also reveals additional structure, since the remaining components of the minimizing vector are shown to have independent probabilistic meaning as limits of distributions of associated generalized eigenvalues.

## 2. Historical Background

The study of the asymptotic spectrum of banded Toeplitz matrices has a long history, originating in the pioneering work of Schmidt and Spitzer in the early 1960s. They considered the case of tridiagonal Toeplitz matrices and showed that the eigenvalues, suitably normalized, converge to a measure supported on an analytic arc in the complex plane, characterized implicitly by a harmonic majorization condition related to the symbol $a(z)$. Their approach combined explicit formulas for the characteristic polynomial with delicate estimates on the location of zeros, and it established for the first time that the limiting spectrum of a non-Hermitian banded Toeplitz matrix is typically a *curve*, rather than a two-dimensional region, in the complex plane—a phenomenon with no counterpart in the Hermitian setting.

Shortly thereafter, Hirschman extended and refined this analysis, placing the problem within the broader framework of the theory of Toeplitz forms and providing sharper asymptotic descriptions of the eigenvalues, including rates of convergence and finer local statistics. Hirschman's contribution clarified the role of the symbol's critical points and of the associated Riemann surface in determining the qualitative features of the limiting curve, laying groundwork that would later be reinterpreted through the lens of potential theory.

In subsequent decades, the connection between the spectral asymptotics of Toeplitz matrices and logarithmic potential theory was made increasingly explicit. It became understood that the eigenvalues of banded Toeplitz matrices can be related, via the resolvent and the associated characteristic equation $\det(T_n(a) - \lambda I) = 0$, to the zeros of certain associated polynomials that arise naturally as solutions of a linear recurrence determined by the symbol. This recurrence, in turn, admits a description in terms of $p+q$ linearly independent solutions corresponding to the roots of $a(z) - \lambda = 0$ for $z$, viewed as functions of the spectral parameter $\lambda$. The resulting multivalued structure gives rise to a Riemann surface of degree $p+q$, and the asymptotic distribution of eigenvalues is intimately tied to harmonic measure and Green's functions on this surface.

## 3. Vector Equilibrium Problems and Multiple Orthogonality

Parallel developments in the theory of Hermite–Padé approximation and multiple orthogonal polynomials introduced the notion of *vector equilibrium problems*, in which one seeks a tuple $(\mu_1, \ldots, \mu_r)$ of probability measures, each supported on a prescribed set (possibly depending on the others), minimizing a joint logarithmic energy functional of the form
$$
E(\mu_1, \ldots, \mu_r) = \sum_{i=1}^{r} \iint \log \frac{1}{|z-w|}\, d\mu_i(z)\, d\mu_i(w) - \sum_{i \neq j} c_{ij} \iint \log \frac{1}{|z-w|} \, d\mu_i(z)\, d\mu_j(w),
$$
subject to fixed total masses and possibly external field contributions, where $(c_{ij})$ is an interaction matrix—often the (inverse) Cartan matrix of a root system such as $A_r$. Such vector equilibrium problems were shown by Gonchar, Rakhmanov, and later authors to govern the zero distributions of multiple orthogonal polynomials, and more generally to arise whenever one studies simultaneous approximation problems involving several interacting families of polynomials, or Riemann surfaces with several sheets glued along common branch points.

It is precisely this framework that provides the natural setting for the eigenvalue problem of banded Toeplitz matrices. Since the eigenvalues of $T_n(a)$ are asymptotically related to the zeros of characteristic polynomials arising from a linear recurrence with $p+q$ characteristic roots, one expects the associated limiting measures to be governed by a vector equilibrium problem on a graph of $p+q-1$ or fewer measures, encoding the mutual interaction between the different sheets of the underlying Riemann surface. The present paper makes this expectation precise.

## 4. Main Results

We formulate an equilibrium problem for vectors of measures $(\mu_1, \ldots, \mu_{p+q-1})$, each $\mu_k$ supported on an admissible compact set determined by the combinatorics of the symbol $a(z)$, subject to a total mass condition reflecting the relative sizes of $p$ and $q$, and interacting through an energy functional built from the logarithmic kernel and an interaction matrix naturally associated with the structure of the characteristic equation. We prove:

* **Existence and uniqueness.** The energy functional admits a unique minimizing vector $(\mu_1^*, \ldots, \mu_{p+q-1}^*)$ within the class of admissible vector measures satisfying the prescribed mass and support constraints.

* **Identification of the spectral measure.** The empirical eigenvalue distribution of $T_n(a)$ converges weak-$*$, as $n \to \infty$, to the first component $\mu_1^*$ of this minimizing vector. This recovers, and considerably generalizes, the arc/curve description obtained by Schmidt–Spitzer and Hirschman, expressing the limiting support as the union of an equilibrium arc determined by an implicit Green's function condition.

* **Interpretation of the remaining components.** The components $\mu_2^*, \ldots, \mu_{p+q-1}^*$ are shown to coincide with the limiting distributions of certain naturally defined *generalized eigenvalues*—specifically, eigenvalues associated with truncations of shifted or dual recurrence relations arising from the same characteristic equation, or equivalently with the zeros of associated families of orthogonal-type polynomials linked to the original Toeplitz recurrence. This provides these auxiliary measures with an independent spectral meaning, rather than treating them merely as auxiliary devices in the equilibrium problem.

* **Variational characterization via Green's functions.** We show that the support of each $\mu_k^*$ and the associated equilibrium conditions can be expressed via a system of Green's function identities on the Riemann surface associated with $a(z) - \lambda$, thereby connecting the vector equilibrium formulation with the classical potential-theoretic description of the limiting spectrum.

## 5. Methodology

Our approach combines several strands of technique. On one hand, we use the classical connection between Toeplitz determinants and the theory of linear difference equations with constant coefficients, following Schmidt–Spitzer and Hirschman, to express $\det(T_n(a) - \lambda I)$ asymptotically in terms of a dominant balance among the roots of $a(z) = \lambda$. On the other hand, we import tools from the theory of vector equilibrium problems and multiple orthogonality, in particular existence and uniqueness results for energy minimizers subject to sign and interaction constraints encoded by a Cartan-type matrix, together with variational (Euler–Lagrange) characterizations in terms of Green's functions and $S$-property conditions for the supports.

A key technical step is the identification of the correct admissible class for the vector of measures—determined by the number of dominant and subdominant roots of the characteristic equation in various asymptotic regimes of $\lambda$—and the verification that the resulting equilibrium problem indeed has the Toeplitz eigenvalue counting function as its first marginal. This requires a careful saddle-point / steepest descent analysis of the relevant determinantal asymptotics, matched against the variational conditions satisfied by the equilibrium measures.

## 6. Organization of the Paper

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. In Section 2 we recall the classical Schmidt–Spitzer and Hirschman theory and set up the relevant linear recurrence and Riemann surface associated with the symbol $a(z)$. Section 3 introduces the vector equilibrium problem, defines the class of admissible measures, and proves existence and uniqueness of the minimizer. Section 4 establishes the main convergence theorem identifying the limiting eigenvalue distribution with the first component of the equilibrium vector. Section 5 develops the interpretation of the remaining components as limiting distributions of generalized eigenvalues, and Section 6 illustrates the theory with explicit examples, including pentadiagonal and other low-order banded symbols, where the equilibrium problem and its solution can be computed explicitly. We conclude with a discussion of extensions to non-banded and perturbed Toeplitz matrices in Section 7.

# Von Toeplitz zu Schmidt: Meilensteine der Funktionalanalysis

Die Entwicklung der modernen Funktionalanalysis zu Beginn des 20. Jahrhunderts ist eng mit den Namen zweier bedeutender Mathematiker verbunden: Otto Toeplitz und Erhard Schmidt. Ihre Arbeiten bildeten wichtige Bausteine auf dem Weg zu einer abstrakten Theorie unendlich-dimensionaler Räume, wie sie später von David Hilbert und seinen Schülern vollständig ausgearbeitet wurde.

## Otto Toeplitz und die unendlichen Matrizen

Otto Toeplitz (1881–1940) beschäftigte sich intensiv mit unendlichen linearen Gleichungssystemen und den dazugehörigen Matrizen. Die nach ihm benannten Toeplitz-Matrizen – Matrizen, deren Einträge entlang jeder Diagonale konstant sind – erwiesen sich als fundamentales Werkzeug in zahlreichen Bereichen der Mathematik, von der Approximationstheorie bis zur Signalverarbeitung. Toeplitz untersuchte systematisch, unter welchen Bedingungen unendliche Matrizen als lineare Operatoren auf Folgenräumen wirken können, und leistete damit einen entscheidenden Beitrag zur Präzisierung des Operatorbegriffs.

## Erhard Schmidt und die Geometrie der Hilberträume

Erhard Schmidt (1876–1959), ein Schüler Hilberts, prägte die geometrische Sichtweise auf unendlich-dimensionale Räume maßgeblich. Sein bekanntestes Vermächtnis ist das Gram-Schmidt-Orthogonalisierungsverfahren, mit dem sich aus einer beliebigen Basis eines Vektorraums eine orthonormale Basis konstruieren lässt. Diese Methode ist heute ein Grundpfeiler der linearen Algebra und findet in der Theorie der Hilberträume ihre natürliche Verallgemeinerung. Auch die Hilbert-Schmidt-Operatoren, eine wichtige Klasse kompakter Operatoren, tragen seinen Namen und spielen eine zentrale Rolle in der Spektraltheorie.

## Der gemeinsame Beitrag

Der Übergang von konkreten, endlich-dimensionalen Betrachtungen hin zu einer abstrakten Theorie unendlich-dimensionaler Räume – der Weg **von** klassischen Matrizenrechnungen **zu** einer vollständig entwickelten Operatortheorie – wurde durch die Arbeiten von Toeplitz und Schmidt entscheidend geebnet. Beide Mathematiker zeigten, wie sich intuitive geometrische und algebraische Konzepte aus der endlichen Dimension sinnvoll auf unendliche Strukturen übertragen lassen. Ihre Beiträge bilden bis heute das Fundament vieler moderner Anwendungen in der Quantenmechanik, der Signalverarbeitung und der numerischen Mathematik.

# Research Abstract

**Title: Potential-Theoretic Analysis of Eigenvalue Accumulation Curves for Banded Toeplitz Matrices: Connections to Schmidt–Spitzer and Hirschman Theory**

We investigate the asymptotic distribution of eigenvalues of large banded Toeplitz matrices through the lens of logarithmic potential theory, establishing refined connections between classical results of Schmidt and Spitzer and complementary work of Hirschman on the spectral behavior of such matrices. It is well known that as the matrix dimension $n \to \infty$, the eigenvalues of a banded Toeplitz matrix $T_n(a)$, generated by a Laurent polynomial symbol $a(z) = \sum_{k=-p}^{q} a_k z^k$, accumulate along a limiting curve $\Gamma_a$ in the complex plane. The Schmidt–Spitzer theorem characterizes this limiting set as the locus where two dominant roots of the equation $a(z) = \lambda$ share equal modulus, while Hirschman's complementary analysis provides sharper information on the density and rate of eigenvalue accumulation along $\Gamma_a$.

In this work, we reinterpret both results within a unified potential-theoretic framework. We show that the accumulation curve $\Gamma_a$ arises naturally as a level set of the Green's function associated with the exterior of a certain compact set determined by the symbol $a(z)$, and that the limiting eigenvalue counting measure coincides with the equilibrium (harmonic) measure on $\Gamma_a$ induced by this potential. This perspective yields a transparent derivation of the Schmidt–Spitzer curve as an algebraic level set of a logarithmic potential, while Hirschman's finer asymptotic density estimates emerge as consequences of the local behavior of the equilibrium measure, governed by the Green's function's normal derivative (via the Cauchy transform) along $\Gamma_a$.

We further examine the interplay between the symbol's algebraic structure—specifically the degrees $p, q$ and coefficient configuration—and the resulting potential-theoretic data, including capacity, equilibrium measure regularity, and rates of convergence for eigenvalues near corners or cusps of $\Gamma_a$. Explicit examples, including tridiagonal and pentadiagonal Toeplitz matrices, illustrate how classical results translate into potential-theoretic language, and we discuss extensions to eigenvalue distributions of non-Hermitian banded Toeplitz matrices under perturbation, variable bandwidth, and non-constant symbol coefficients (locally Toeplitz structures). Our results provide a bridge between the operator-theoretic and potential-theoretic approaches to non-Hermitian spectral asymptotics, offering new tools for analyzing pseudospectra and eigenvalue clustering in large structured matrices arising in numerical analysis, statistical mechanics, and random matrix theory.

**Keywords:** Toeplitz matrices, eigenvalue distribution, logarithmic potential theory, Schmidt–Spitzer theorem, equilibrium measure, non-Hermitian spectral asymptotics

We study the limiting spectral distribution of banded Toeplitz matrices through the lens of vector equilibrium problems. It is classically known that the empirical eigenvalue distribution of a sequence of banded Toeplitz matrices converges weakly to the pushforward, under the associated symbol, of the uniform measure on the unit circle. We show that this limiting spectral measure arises naturally as one component of a vector equilibrium measure defined on several intervals or contours in the complex plane, with the remaining components governing the asymptotic distribution of generalized eigenvalues associated to the underlying banded matrix problem.

Specifically, we reformulate the eigenvalue problem for banded Toeplitz matrices in terms of a system of orthogonal polynomials satisfying a higher-order recurrence relation, whose asymptotic zero distribution is characterized by a vector equilibrium problem with an upper constraint on one measure and mutual interaction (via an inverse Cauchy-type matrix) between the components. This unified variational framework not only reproduces known results on the spectra of banded Toeplitz matrices but also extends them by placing the eigenvalue asymptotics in the broader context of multiple orthogonal polynomials and vector potential theory, thereby clarifying the interaction between the geometry of the symbol's image curve and the equilibrium measures' supports. We illustrate the theory with explicit examples for small bandwidths, showing how the vector equilibrium problem decouples the classical limiting measure from the finer asymptotic structure of the generalized eigenvalues, and we discuss implications for the study of non-Hermitian Toeplitz and banded Hankel operators more generally.

# Abstract

We investigate the asymptotic distribution of eigenvalues of Toeplitz matrices generated by symbols arising as products of algebraic functions and Fisher-Hartwig singularities, extending classical results of Szegő and Widom to a broader class of non-Hermitian and non-Hermitian-adjacent settings. Our approach reformulates the eigenvalue counting problem in terms of a vector equilibrium problem posed on a system of curves and contours in the complex plane, where the interaction between component measures is governed by a matrix of interaction coefficients determined by the branching structure of the underlying symbol.

We establish that as the matrix dimension $n \to \infty$, the empirical eigenvalue distribution converges weakly to the balayage of a reference measure onto the union of these contours, characterized as the unique solution to the associated vector equilibrium problem with mixed constraints. The support of this limiting measure is identified via a Riemann surface construction naturally associated to the symbol, and we derive an explicit description of the limiting contours through a system of algebraic equations reminiscent of trajectories of quadratic differentials.

Key to our analysis is a Riemann-Hilbert framework adapted to matrix-valued orthogonal polynomials associated with the symbol, from which we extract strong asymptotics for the eigenvalues, including precise rate of convergence estimates and a characterization of the limiting eigenvalue counting function in terms of the equilibrium potential. We further establish universality results describing the local eigenvalue statistics near regular points of the limiting support, showing that they coincide with the sine-kernel process, while at singular points of the symbol (including Fisher–Hartwig-type singularities) a new family of local statistics emerges, governed by a confluent hypergeometric kernel.

As applications, we recover and sharpen known results for banded Toeplitz matrices and Toeplitz matrices with rational symbols, resolve several conjectures concerning the spectra of non-Hermitian random Toeplitz-like operators, and provide a unified explanation for previously observed numerical phenomena regarding eigenvalue clustering along non-trivial arcs. Our results demonstrate that the vector equilibrium problem framework, originally developed for multiple orthogonal polynomials, provides a natural and powerful language for understanding spectral asymptotics of structured non-normal matrices.
